items.title: Exploring Pre-Service English Language Teachers’ Silence and Engagement in an Oral Communication Class
items.abstract: This study explores how first-year pre-service English language teachers (PSELTs) interpret classroom silence and engagement in an Oral Communication course and how they understand their own participation after comparison with a more participatory course section. Theoretically, it brings Willingness to Communicate (WTC) and Oral Communication Apprehension (OCA) into dialogue with a multidimensional engagement framework while treating silence as behavior whose meaning must be interpreted rather than assumed. Using a qualitative exploratory design, the study involved 48 PSELTs in two pre-existing, administratively constituted course sections taught by the same instructor under the same syllabus. Data were generated through an open-ended questionnaire, written self-reflections, individual semi-structured interviews with 15 focal-section participants, and post-comparison written reflections. Two combined-class sessions provided the comparison, with the more participatory section serving as a contextual point of comparison rather than a baseline or control group. Findings showed that participants associated silence most strongly with fear of negative evaluation and perfectionism, alongside linguistic retrieval difficulties, limited topic knowledge, peer relations, low interest, attentional drift, fatigue, prior learning experiences, and conditions beyond the classroom. Conversely, a smaller set of accounts described silence as active listening, cognitive processing, or preparation for later participation, indicating that limited observable participation can coexist with cognitive engagement. Notably, post-comparison accounts gave greater prominence to relationships, teamwork, and classroom climate, although similar social explanations were already evident before the comparison activity. The findings therefore support a shift in emphasis rather than a causal change in engagement or WTC. Ultimately, OCA explains an important part of silence among PSELTs but not its full range of conditions and functions. The study concludes that silence in language teacher education is heterogeneous, situated, and analytically ambiguous. Teacher educators should distinguish observable quietness from disengagement while attending to the affective, cognitive, relational, and contextual conditions that shape participation.

items.title: Exploring the Limits of the Delta Learning Hypothesis: Single-Pair Generator Biases in Direct Preference Optimization
items.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) typically relies on preference pairs generated from diverse model pools and ranked by an external LLM judge. The recently proposed delta-learning hypothesis suggests that comparable supervision can instead be obtained from a single pair of models by treating the larger model's response as preferred. We investigate the limits of this approach across model families and scales. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that fixed model pairs introduce systematic, generator-dependent biases that are predictive of the preference label independent of response quality. Consequently, DPO trained on single-pair data consistently underperforms multi-model preference data, despite the larger generator producing higher-quality responses, and we trace this gap to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases. We further show that simply increasing the number of generators, even without an external judge, is enough to partially mitigate this effect. Our results highlight generator diversity as a critical factor in preference-data construction.

items.title: Feature-Aware Test Generation for Deep Learning Models
items.abstract: As deep learning (DL) models are widely used in software systems, test generation plays a crucial role in assessing the quality of such models before deployment. To date, the most advanced test generators rely on generative AI to synthesize inputs; however, these approaches remain limited in providing semantic insight into the causes of misbehaviours and in offering fine-grained semantic controllability over the generated inputs. In this paper, we introduce Detect, a feature-aware test generation framework for vision-based DL models that generates inputs by perturbing disentangled semantic attributes within the latent space. Detect perturbs individual latent features in a controlled way and observes how these changes affect the model’s output. Through this process, it identifies which features lead to behaviour shifts and uses a vision-language model for semantic attribution. Detect enables semantically controlled perturbations in StyleGAN’s disentangled latent space, allowing us to test whether a model generalizes under task-relevant feature changes and remains invariant under task-irrelevant ones. Empirical results across image classification and detection tasks show that Detect generates high-quality test cases with fine-grained control, reveals distinct shortcut behaviours across model architectures (convolutional and transformer-based), and bugs that are not captured by accuracy metrics. Specifically, Detect outperforms a state-of-the-art test generator in decision boundary discovery and provides more interpretable feature-level diagnoses than a leading spurious feature localization method in identifying robustness failures. Our findings show that fully fine-tuned convolutional models are prone to overfitting on localized cues, such as co-occurring visual traits, while weakly supervised transformers tend to rely on global features, such as environmental variances. These findings highlight the value of interpretable and feature-aware testing in improving DL model reliability, and refocus DL testing from class-level failure discovery to feature-level, semantically grounded diagnosis and repair.

items.title: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features
items.abstract: A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.

items.title: FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision
items.abstract: Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce \textbf{FilingLoop}, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical U.S.\ Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from 24.28\% to 27.96\% and full comment resolution from 16.90\% to 20.75\%, with a 5.8\% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.

items.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
items.abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

items.title: Follow the Herd: A Data-Driven Approach for Actionable Recourse
items.abstract: As machine learning systems make increasingly greater decisions about people's lives, it is critical to provide users with actionable recourse about how they can achieve their desired outcomes. This problem is currently tackled by relying on expensive human supervision which involves hand-designing a cost function before searching for low-cost actions that achieve the desired outcome. In this paper, we propose \textit{``Data-Driven Action Recourse"} (DDAR), the first approach for providing action recourse without requiring costly supervision from humans about action costs. We build upon the notion that highly likely trajectories in the historical user data should be associated with lower costs. With this, DDAR first builds a dynamics model of historical user trajectories. Under this model, it then searches for trajectories that achieve the desired outcome. In experiments, we find that this simple approach recommends plausible action recourse without requiring human supervision, achieving lower action costs than the existing approaches.

items.title: Foot Biomechanics, Body Composition, and Sex‐Related Factors Associated With Work‐Related Musculoskeletal Discomfort in Standing Assembly‐Line Workers: A Cross‐Sectional Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prolonged standing is common in manufacturing and assembly-line work and is associated with musculoskeletal discomfort, especially in the lower limbs and spine. The influence of foot posture, morphology, and plantar loading patterns on this discomfort remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To analyze the associations between foot posture, plantar pressure, and 3D foot morphology with work-related musculoskeletal discomfort in standing workers and to examine the role of BMI and the potential modifying role of sex. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 240 assembly-line workers (129 women, 53.8%). Musculoskeletal discomfort was assessed using the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ). Foot posture (FPI-6), baropodometry (FreeMed), and 3D foot morphology (DOMESCAN) were evaluated under standardized conditions. Participants were classified as having low (CMDQ ≤ 10) or moderate-high (≥ 11) discomfort. Firth-penalized logistic regression analyzed associations between overall CMDQ discomfort, foot posture, sex, and BMI, including an FPI × sex interaction term. RESULTS: All workers reported at least one musculoskeletal discomfort response, with the feet, neck, and lumbar region accounting for the largest proportions of reported discomfort. Among women, pronated foot posture was associated with higher odds of moderate-high overall CMDQ discomfort (OR = 2.91, 95% CI 1.10-7.28). Overweight/obesity status was associated with higher odds of foot and hip/gluteal discomfort, whereas, among women, pronated foot posture was associated with greater odds of lumbar discomfort. The pronation-discomfort association was stronger in women and attenuated in men. CONCLUSIONS: Among women, pronated foot posture was associated with greater overall work-related musculoskeletal discomfort during prolonged standing and with greater odds of lumbar discomfort, whereas overweight/obesity status was associated with greater odds of foot and hip/gluteal discomfort. The pronation-discomfort association was attenuated in men. From an occupational-health perspective, incorporating foot-posture and BMI assessment into ergonomic evaluations may help identify workers who could benefit from more individualized preventive strategies, particularly women with pronated feet.

items.title: From Design Principles to Practice: Validation of a UX Design Checklist for Affective Conversational Agents in Mental Well-Being
items.abstract: University students' psychological well-being is a critical public health concern, creating demand for digital interventions that are both safe and effective. Although conversational agents offer scalable support, existing usability heuristics cannot address complex affective dimensions such as emotional containment and clinical safety, revealing a gap in specialized design frameworks. To address this, the study introduces the “Affective Design Checklist,” a practical inspection tool for developing and auditing mental health conversational agents. Using Jabareen's conceptual framework analysis with a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 43 key articles, the instrument underwent a two-stage validation by a panel of ten experts, achieving a scale-level Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave) of 0.971, with near-unanimous agreement on ethical and regulatory dimensions. This research translates abstract bioethical and affective computing principles into actionable verification items, offering a specialized standard to ensure digital interventions are technically usable, affectively competent, and ethically aligned with student needs.

items.title: From digital access to workforce capability: a comparative documentary study of AI-relevant learning ecosystems in Singapore, Europe and India
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is typically linked to the learning platform, the diagnosis of skills and employment services, but the advantages of AI to workforce training are still not even as the skills acquired in the learning platform are not automatically available for use. There is already a significant amount of published work that discusses automation risk, as well as digital competencies and the role of AI in learning and development, but less comparative focus on the institutions that transform learning resources into recognised skills and employability through the operation and use of AI enabled and/or AI relevant learning environments. By designing it around the theoretically motivated Capability Approach of Sen, this study analyzed SkillsFuture Singapore and the European Digital Skills and Jobs Coalition and India’s National Career Service using a qualitative comparative documentary approach. Thematic analysis was performed using secondary data such as all documents of platforms, official documents, intergovernmental document and peer-reviewed literature, which were publicly available and interpreted each case one by one as a documentary thematic analysis. It suggests that the strength of workforce-learning ecosystems emerges when combined with trying to make digital accessible, within an affordable context, with digital skills, counselling, assisted access, language-sensitive design, recognition by employers, transparency in governance, and evidence of outcomes. With Singapore demonstrating coordinated lifelong learning, Europe demonstrates the good and bad of mobilising digital skills across multiple stakeholders and levels and India helps to show how to apply the reach of platforms to employment-related skills inclusion at large scale. The analysis of the study presents a framework for capability conversion, which attempts to simultaneously analyze the AI-relevant workforce's learning, even though the mere presence of the platform does not guarantee it is effective. The shocks are not "user" shocks or "platform-internal" shocks because of the documentary nature of the evidence, which leaves room for analytical interpretations of the findings as more representative of outcomes in the labour market rather than causal interpretations.

items.abstract: This case study critically examines the evolution of the metaverse, interrogating its ascendancy, its perceived decline and the nascent indicators of its resurgence. Beginning with the concept’s origins in science fiction, it tracks the metaverse’s evolution through advancements in gaming and the growing interest of Big Tech, which saw potential in this convergence of virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR) and mixed reality (MR). The narrative captures the initial exuberance as investors and companies raced to stake their claim, buoyed by forecasts of a new era of digital interaction and economic activity.Looking at the nature of the sector and the ecosystems it fostered, the case considers what drove inflated expectations and subsequent market corrections. It explores the sobering challenges that faced the metaverse: technological limitations, user disillusionment and a harsh economic climate that eroded speculative investments. It discusses the strategic shifts by key players, from pursuit of domination to focused niches and smart partnerships, and the downsizing or redirection of metaverse initiatives in response to the market’s reality checks. It also identifies emerging signs of vitality in the sector. It highlights how the integration of generative AI (GenAI) and targeted applications in gaming are rekindling interest, suggesting a potential pathway out of disillusionment.The case also provides the opportunity to track the emergence of multiple partly overlapping ecosystems and allows students to focus on the different roles and monetisation approaches that ecosystem participants take. It further allows us to see the upsides and downsides of more centralised ecosystems (like those driven by Big Tech) and more decentralised ecosystems (such as Web3) and consider how the ecosystem orchestrators try to leverage their strengths. The case can also be used to consider in what ways orchestrators benefit more broadly.

items.title: From LC-MS Metabolomic Profiling to AIEnabled Navigation of NPs Chemical Space: Recent Advances and Emerging Directions
items.abstract: Natural products (NPs) occupy a unique region of chemical space and continue to provide privileged scaffolds for drug discovery, chemical ecology, and biotechnology. However, the exploration of NP diversity remains constrained by the complexity of biological extracts, the low annotation rate of LC-MS features, and the rediscovery of known metabolites. Recent advances in LC-HRMS/MS-based metabolomics, coupled with expanding spectral and structural databases, molecular networking, and in silico annotation methods, have considerably improved the characterization of complex metabolomes and facilitated large-scale exploration of natural chemical space. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning approaches are enhancing metabolite annotation, chemical classification, and prioritization, while knowledge graph technologies enable the integration of chemical, taxonomic, biological, and ecological information into interoperable, AI-ready frameworks. This mini-review highlights recent developments that support a transition from conventional metabolite annotation towards effective navigation of NP chemical space. We discuss the role of open data resources, computational metabolomics, knowledge-driven data integration, and emerging AI-assisted tools in accelerating NP discovery. We also examine how biotransformation and chemoenzymatic diversification can extend the boundaries of natural chemical space by generating nature-inspired molecules and previously inaccessible scaffolds. Together, these approaches are paving the way towards a more predictive, integrative, and data-driven paradigm for NP research and bioactive compound discovery.

items.title: From orchestra to classroom: learner-centered music training as a tool to support motivation to learn
items.abstract: Fostering more self-determined forms of motivation in students remains a key challenge in education. According to self-determination theory (SDT), educational environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness enhance more autonomous forms of motivation. Music education in collaborative, learner-centered formats may provide such conditions. This study investigates whether participation in learner-centered orchestral training is associated with changes in children's general academic motivation.The study involved 113 children aged 8–10 years. Half joined a three-month orchestral program emphasizing active participation, peer collaboration, and public performance. The other half formed a control group with no music training. Motivation was assessed pre- and post-training using the Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire.Children in the music group showed a greater reduction in external regulation compared to the control group. For intrinsic motivation, a descriptive trend toward improvement was observed in the music group relative to the control group, although the Group x Time interaction did not reach statistical significance.These findings suggest that learner-centered orchestral training may support a shift towards more self-determined forms of motivation, primarily through reduced external regulation.

items.title: From Proposal to Discovery: Attribution, Validation, and Responsibility in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Science / De la propuesta al descubrimiento: atribución, validación y responsabilidad en la ciencia asistida por inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: ENGLISH This critical conceptual essay examines how to distinguish a proposed AI-assisted scientific discovery from its validation, the documented contributions of participants, and responsibility for communicating the result. It develops a four-register framework covering the scientific claim, the standard of evidence attained, the provenance of contributions, and communication responsibility. Published examples illustrate why generating hypotheses or computational results is not, by itself, equivalent to validating all claims made about them. The essay reports no original experiment or systematic review; the proposed framework has not been empirically validated. This record contains the complete English and Spanish editions, Version 1.0. Desarrolla un marco de cuatro registros: afirmación científica, estándar de prueba alcanzado, procedencia de las contribuciones y responsabilidad comunicativa. Los ejemplos publicados ilustran por qué generar hipótesis o resultados computacionales no equivale por sí solo a validar todas las afirmaciones derivadas de ellos. items.title: From Ripple to Boundary: Deterministic Impact Boundaries for LLM-Based Software Evolution
items.abstract: The landscape of software evolution is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift in the era of Large Language Models. As industrial software engineering increasingly transitions toward design-driven code generation, the bottleneck of evolution has shifted from writing code to maintaining deterministic consistency between multi-source design assets and the generated code. When a design asset changes, LLM agents currently lack a deterministic impact boundary to identify which code must be evolved, leading to two failure modes: hallucinating missing changes or breaking unrelated code. Probabilistic approaches, such as semantic retrieval or text-based diffing, fail to capture the structural ripple effects across highly interconnected design dependencies. We propose a paradigm shift from probabilistic semantic retrieval to deterministic structural constraints. We formalize the design assets as a Knowledge Graph and organize them into a content-addressed Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph. Our key insight reveals a topological isomorphism between the logical ripple effect of a design change and the content hash propagation within the DAG. By leveraging this, we transform ambiguous impact analysis into verifiable structural operations. Through a two-phase diffing process, we extract a precise causal chain that defines the exact modification boundary. This boundary enables deterministic context injection, providing the LLM agent with strictly scoped code and design updates, thereby fundamentally guaranteeing evolution safety. As a by-product, the KG serves as an agent-queryable knowledge base for natural language design retrieval. Early deployment on a large-scale industrial payment platform demonstrates that our mechanism successfully computes the exact impact boundary and generates incremental code modifications that meet the expected design changes.

items.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.

items.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

items.title: GarmentSegAgent: Autonomous Garment Segmentation for Web Fashion Images via Textual Self-Refinement
items.abstract: Web fashion images support applications such as visual product search and consumer-to-shop matching, yet their visual heterogeneity makes reliable garment segmentation challenging. Despite advances in promptable segmentation, autonomously identifying and correcting garment-specific errors without human-provided spatial prompts remains difficult. We propose GarmentSegAgent, an autonomous framework that integrates semantic planning, spatial execution, and visual evaluation through iterative textual self-refinement. At its core, we introduce CAST (Constrained Attribution-guided Selective TextGrad), which connects visual error attribution with targeted textual optimization. CAST identifies instruction components responsible for segmentation errors, selectively updates them through textual gradients, and validates the resulting instructions against garment-specific constraints. This enables image-specific error correction at inference time while keeping the underlying foundation models frozen. Experiments on DeepFashion2, ModaNet, and Fashionpedia demonstrate consistent improvements in region overlap and boundary accuracy, alongside more reliable refinement than conventional TextGrad. By enabling visual feedback to guide controlled instruction updates, GarmentSegAgent offers a promising direction for autonomous garment understanding, with potential applications in scalable fashion content analysis, visual retrieval, and consumer-to-shop matching on the Web.

items.title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

items.title: Generative AI Drives a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery: An Analysis of Technical Approaches, Application Cases, and Challenges
items.abstract: Traditional drug research and development has long been characterised by long development cycles, high investment costs and a high attrition rate among candidate compounds, conventional experimental methods for screening candidate compounds are of limited efficiency when faced with the vast chemical space and complex biological mechanisms. Generative artificial intelligence can provide a new technological approach to new drug research and development by generating conditions based on the distribution patterns of molecular structures and their properties, and by enabling de novo molecular design. This paper systematically reviews the main generative models—including RNNs, Transformers, VAEs, GANs, normalising flows and diffusion models—and their technical characteristics. It analyses their applications in drug target discovery, protein structure prediction, candidate compound generation and lead optimisation, with a particular focus on how generative AI, when combined with active learning, computational physics and feedback from wet-lab experiments, reshapes the drug discovery and development process. Research indicates that generative AI, when combined with active learning, physical computing and feedback from wet-lab experiments, is driving a shift in drug discovery from the traditional linear open-loop model towards a data-driven iterative model of 'generation–evaluation–feedback–regeneration–experimental validation'. By examining the technical characteristics of various generative models and their suitability for drug discovery tasks, this paper provides guidance on selecting generative AI technologies, identifying suitable application scenarios and integrating them into drug discovery workflows.

items.title: Generative AI use in entrepreneurship: An integrative review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. The future of entrepreneurship will depend less on whether entrepreneurs use GenAI than on how they use it. Used thoughtfully, GenAI may empower entrepreneurs by expanding their capabilities to engage in entrepreneurial activities. Used uncritically, GenAI may entrap entrepreneurs by restricting or eroding those capabilities. Entrepreneurs should therefore verify what GenAI produces, calibrate GenAI use to their expertise and task demands, and decide which tasks to delegate to GenAI while retaining human judgment for consequential decisions.

items.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $τ$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

items.title: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.

items.title: Governing AI Coding Agents: An Empirical Analysis of Repository Artifacts
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Software projects are increasingly using repository-level governance artifacts, such as \texttt{CLAUDE.md} and \texttt{AGENTS.md}, to communicate project-specific guidance to AI coding agents. Although these artifacts have become an important mechanism for governing AI coding agents, little is known about the governance practices and liabilities they encode, or whether their observable characteristics are consistent with organizational governance capability. Method: To examine these questions, we conducted an exploratory sequential mixed-methods study of 555 AI agent governance artifacts collected from public GitHub repositories. Using Socio-Technical Grounded Theory for Data Analysis (STGT4DA), we developed taxonomies of governance practices and governance liabilities, which were converted into a structured codebook for LLM-based classification. The codebook was evaluated against manually coded reference labels and applied to the corpus to examine whether these artifacts exhibit observable characteristics theoretically associated with organizational governance capability. Results: The findings reveal that these artifacts primarily emphasize knowledge transfer, process guidance, and coding standards, whereas explicit oversight mechanisms, such as human approval gates, remain comparatively limited. The analysis also identifies recurring governance liabilities, most commonly vague instructions (36%) and fragmentation debt (35%). We found no systematic association between the governance observed in the artifacts and the repository maturity indicators examined in this study, nor did governance vary systematically across the application domains examined as broad proxies for potential operational consequences. The artifacts also showed limited evidence of characteristics associated with institutionalized governance, particularly regarding accountability mechanisms, coherence between governance content and governance quality, and project-specific adaptation. Conclusion: This study provides an empirical investigation of repository-level AI agent governance from an organizational capability perspective. By examining governance artifacts according to the governance functions they perform rather than solely the information they contain, the study develops taxonomies of governance practices and liabilities and an evaluated LLM-based classification approach for systematically characterizing AI agent governance in research and practice.

items.title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
items.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.

items.title: GraphRAGProv: GraphRAG Meets How-Provenance
items.abstract: GraphRAG systems often use knowledge graphs to retrieve relevant context for an LLM that produces the final answer. That makes answers more inscrutable and therefore less appealing for domains where transparency is paramount. We present GraphRAGProv, an architecture that executes SPARQL queries over source-grounded RDF graphs to compute answers and their how-provenance polynomials. These polynomials record which statement occurrences were used and how they were combined. Because each occurrence is linked to its source text, users can follow these links to check whether the extracted statements reflect the text and whether the query combines them to answer the question. Querying thereby becomes a way to inspect and evaluate the text-to-graph transformation. Our interactive demo examines 400 cases from two multi-hop QA benchmarks, revealing extraction and query errors even when the final answer is correct.

items.abstract: This evidence-based practice project explored structured group activities to support cognitive engagement, social interaction, and well-being among assisted living and memory care residents with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias. Drawing on cognitive stimulation, reminiscence, and Montessori-based care, recommendations included music, memory games, creative activities, and meaningful daily tasks adapted to residents’ interests and abilities. items.title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.

items.title: Hidden vulnerabilities, ethical concerns and governance issues in advanced cryptography for intelligent healthcare systems
items.abstract: Despite advancements in cryptographic techniques such as homomorphic encryption, blockchain, attribute-based encryption and quantum-resistant algorithms that aim to enhance privacy and trust in healthcare, significant ethical and technical issues remain. This chapter fills that gap by systematically examining vulnerabilities related to algorithmic logic, mathematical fragility, randomness generation and human misimplementation. Using case studies from real and simulated healthcare environments, it explores how encryption mistakes, biased artificial intelligence (AI) generated keys or restricted data access can threaten both patients and healthcare providers. The findings align with existing security standards, indicating that cryptographic failures are often sociotechnical rather than purely technical problems. The chapter emphasises that protecting patient data effectively requires not only technical solutions but also ethical governance frameworks that promote transparency, continuous auditing and human oversight in the design of cryptography. Looking ahead, the chapter underscores the importance of incorporating ethics-by-design principles and fostering collaboration among engineers, ethicists and policymakers to ensure future healthcare cryptography safeguards both digital security and human dignity.

items.title: How control allocation in AI-enabled travel planning shapes reuse intention: the roles of user experience, emotion regulation and psychological empowerment
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how control allocation between users and artificial intelligence (AI) systems shapes reuse intention in AI-enabled travel planning and whether this effect operates through user experience (UX), cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, psychological empowerment and satisfaction. Design/methodology/approach Two scenario-based studies were conducted. A laboratory pilot (n = 92) validated system-dominant, shared-control and user-dominant planning conditions. A main online study (n = 463) tested the proposed serial process using confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrapping. Findings Control allocation significantly affected UX. More favorable UX increased cognitive reappraisal and reduced expressive suppression, and these two regulatory routes had opposite effects on psychological empowerment. Empowerment enhanced satisfaction, which subsequently predicted reuse intention. A supplementary analysis further indicated that AI usage experience conditioned the relationships between UX and emotion regulation. Practical implications AI travel planners should treat control allocation as an interaction-design decision. Modular editing, progressive explanations, reversible changes and adaptive control can preserve user agency while retaining the efficiency benefits of AI assistance. Originality/value This study extends continuance research by identifying the upstream psychological process through which satisfaction is formed under different control-allocation structures. It further distinguishes UX as an evaluative appraisal from emotion regulation as a subsequent coping process in AI-enabled travel planning.

items.title: How Does Horizontal-Curve Radius Affect Drivers’ Visual and Psychophysiological Load? Evidence from an On-Road Driving Experiment
items.abstract: An on-road experiment with 27 drivers across 50 horizontal curves examined the association between radius and visual psychophysiological workload on a mountainous two-lane highway. Pupil-area change rate, fixation intensity, heart-rate change rate, and heart-rate variability (SDNN) were combined using factor analysis and entropy weighting. Crossed linear mixed-effects models used driver and curve section as random intercepts and radius as a continuous predictor. Smaller radii were generally associated with higher pupil, fixation, and heart-rate responses and lower SDNN. Among linear, quadratic, cubic, and logarithmic forms, the logarithmic comprehensive-load model fit best (AIC = −2511.47; BIC = −2485.43), with a significant radius effect (β = −0.2968, 95% CI: −0.3283 to −0.2653, p < 0.001). Successive-curve inconsistency was not independently significant (p = 0.976). Within 45.83–900.83 m, exploratory workload boundaries were approximately 75, 150, 270, and 500 m. These are preliminary human-factors screening values, not design standards or validated comfort thresholds.

items.title: How to engage disabled and older people with technology
items.abstract: Whilst technology has the potential to deliver significant benefits to older and disabled people, enabling greater mobility and independence, it may also leave them unable or unwilling to engage with it, or lacking in trust. Understanding how people engage with technology in relation to their mobility is the core aim of this chapter. To understand how people engage with technology, we need to know who they are and enough about them to understand how and why they do or do not engage, and we also need to know about the features of the technology that encourage or discourage engagement. Thus, part 1 addresses older people and how they think and behave in relation to technology; this includes their motivation, attitudes and beliefs and how their cognitive abilities interact with possible uses of technology and whether there is a digital divide. Part 2 addresses the issues associated with the technology that make it easier or harder to use, and more or less likely for people to engage with; this includes what we know about how people actually engage in terms of ergonomics, which includes the perceptual and cognitive elements of the technology.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Language Assessment: EFL Learners' Trust, Anxiety, and AI Literacy in AI-Mediated Writing Feedback
items.abstract: This study aimed to examine how EFL learners' trust in AI feedback, AI-related anxiety, and AI literacy relate to their engagement with, and uptake of, AI-mediated written corrective feedback. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined survey data from 300 university EFL learners, analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), with follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 16); the structural model explained 48% of the variance in feedback uptake. AI literacy positively predicted trust (β = .46) and negatively predicted anxiety (β = -.39); trust was the strongest positive predictor of both engagement (β = .41) and uptake (β = .44), while anxiety exerted smaller negative effects. A cluster analysis identified three learner profiles - Confident Collaborators, Anxious Verifiers, and Detached Low-Literacy Users. Because anxiety was measured at three points across the period of AI-mediated collaboration, change over time was also examined: a repeated-measures ANOVA showed AI anxiety declining significantly across the three waves (partial η² = .18), and a latent growth curve model showed that higher AI literacy and higher trust each predicted a steeper decline. The qualitative findings showed that learners did not accept AI feedback uncritically but practised calibrated trust, verifying machine feedback against teachers and peers, and that AI literacy functioned as a regulating resource that tempered both over-reliance and anxiety. On this basis the study proposes a Calibrated Trust Framework for AI-mediated assessment, in which AI literacy supports calibrated trust, calibrated trust drives engagement, and engagement converts into uptake. The study advances a learner-centred account of human-AI collaboration in language assessment and argues that AI literacy, rather than tool sophistication alone, is central to responsible, pedagogically meaningful, AI-mediated assessment. Implications for assessment design, teacher education, and ethical practice are discussed.

items.title: Human-centered AI Capability and employee outcomes in an emerging economy: mediating role of empowerment and moderating role of digital culture
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational life, yet whether and how this technology benefits employees remains poorly understood, particularly in emerging economies where digital transformation is proceeding rapidly but unevenly. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Psychological Empowerment Theory, this study examines how organizational AI capability relates to employee performance and engagement and asks whether psychological empowerment channels this relationship and whether digital organizational culture strengthens or weakens it. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 387 employees across 42 organizations in Egypt spanning the banking, telecommunications, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail sectors, and were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation tests and multi-group comparisons. AI capability was positively associated with both employee performance and engagement, and employee empowerment partially mediated these relationships, indicating that AI's benefits for employees flow substantially through employees' sense of autonomy, competence, and impact rather than through technology alone. Digital organizational culture moderated this pathway: the AI capability-to-empowerment relationship was roughly twice as strong in organizations with a well-developed digital culture as in those without one. These findings extend the Resource-Based View to the individual level, position empowerment as a key psychological mechanism linking organizational AI resources to human outcomes and demonstrate that AI's human benefits are culturally and organizationally contingent rather than automatic. The results contribute emerging-economy evidence to a literature dominated by developed-country studies and offer practical guidance for organizations seeking to deploy AI in ways that empower, rather than sideline, their workforce.

items.title: Human-Centered, Non-Invasive Brain-to-AI Interfacing (B2AI): A Proof-of-Concept Feasibility Case Study in Augmented Cognition
items.abstract: Brain-to-AI Interfacing (B2AI) offers a novel human-centered neurotechnology framework for augmented cognition. In this proof-of-concept feasibility case study, we demonstrate a working non-invasive B2AI prototype supporting bidirectional communication between a user and a large language model (LLM) through EEG-based input and TMS-based feedback. In a virtual navigation task, we found that use of the B2AI system was associated with higher path efficiency in a single-user case study. Additionally, we found that the average time per step was higher when the system was active, likely reflecting the time required to initiate the EEG command, query the AI module, receive TMS feedback, and execute the instructed movement. Together, these findings suggest that the B2AI system was technically feasible and may support more efficient task performance under constrained experimental conditions. Future work and fully powered experiments will be needed to determine the generalizability, usability, safety, and application value of the system, but this case study suggests that current technology supports the use of B2AI as an experimental tool for augmented cognition research.

items.title: Human-Centric HRC for Agriculture]{Design and Validation of a Human-Centric Human--Robot Collaboration System for Agriculture Using an AI-Driven Digital Twin
items.abstract: Abstract UK agriculture is facing an acute labour shortage, particularly on small farms where unpredictable and unstructured environments make automation difficult. Although robotic systems offer promising solutions, fully autonomous approaches remain costly and complex to implement. Human--Robot Collaboration provides a more practical alternative by combining human judgement with robotic assistance. This study investigates how digital twin-based simulation platforms can be designed to effectively model and optimise collaboration between humans and robots in complex agricultural settings. It also examines the performance trade-offs in vision and gesture-based collaboration systems, focusing on the balance between speed, accuracy and robustness, and explores the safety challenges related to recognising human intent and ensuring safe adaptive behaviour.To address these issues, a digital twin framework was constructed using the NVIDIA Omniverse platform, enabling the simulation of collaborative agricultural scenarios. The virtual testbed includes dynamic farm layouts, human models, and mobile robots equipped with RGB and LiDAR sensors to interpret gestures and actions with AI and a Vision-Language Model. Experimental results show high human detection accuracy (intersection over union up to 97%) and reliable robot responses to human guidance. This research presents the first virtual environment in agriculture that integrates human factors and intelligent robotic reasoning. The proposed framework provides a scalable, low-risk approach for developing, testing and optimising collaborative robotic systems, supporting wider adoption of intelligent automation in the farming sector.

items.title: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as automated judges, yet most alignment methods target aggregated human judgments and overlook variation among individual annotators. Existing approaches to matching the full distribution of human ratings mainly rely on output-level calibration or parameter fine-tuning. We propose Human-Residual Steering (HRS), to our knowledge the first method to align frozen LLM judges with human judgment distributions through learned hidden-state interventions. An oracle analysis shows that low-rank corrections at a single layer remove most of the discrepancy between judge and human distributions. HRS learns to predict such corrections from the judge's hidden representation and rating logits, training on individual annotations with proper scoring rules for ordinal and nominal judgments and optimising through the frozen downstream layers. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, HRS outperforms all evaluated frozen-weight baselines. With Qwen2.5-7B, it achieves the lowest Jensen-Shannon distance on 13 of 14 benchmarks, reducing the mean from 0.565 to 0.352 versus 0.377 for the strongest calibrator. HRS also raises mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores from 0.449 to 0.579, improves population-level estimation under limited annotation budgets, and trains about 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest cost in alignment.

items.title: Identifying Reasons behind Climate Change Denial: A Study on the YouTube Social Media
items.abstract: Abstract Climate change and global warming have become a great threat to the human race. However, a significant part of the global population continues to deny the severity of climate change. To effectively raise awareness, create policies, and design interventions, it is important to examine the nuanced reasons behind such denial. To the best of our knowledge, prior research has not classified social media posts based on specific reasons for rejecting the claim that climate change or global warming is a serious concern. In this work, we use open-weight large language models (LLMs) for detecting climate change denial-related comments. Additionally, LLMs are applied for multi-label classification of social media content to uncover specific reasons for climate change denial.Our experiments suggest that an ensemble of LLMs performs better in this classification task, than individual models in a zero-shot setting. Further, our findings reveal that believing the global warming as a conspiracy theory and perceiving climate change as a natural phenomenon are the most common themes in denial narratives. We also analyze how the various themes co-occur, showing how different forms of denial support each other within individual comments.

items.title: Ignore the Writing: A Proposal for Peer Review in the Age of AI
items.abstract: The written paper has long stood in as proof of work: a fluent, well-structured manuscript was taken as evidence that good research lay behind it. Generative AI has broken that link. Polished manuscripts now cost nothing to produce, submissions are outgrowing what reviewers can absorb, and venues are turning to AI for help. The logical endpoint is a loop where AI writes the papers and AI reviews them. We argue that this loop is survivable, but only if it is given a reward function, and that human reviewing effort should become that reward function. We propose that submissions should consist of a 1500-word brief plus an unlimited, machine-verifiable appendix. Human reviewers judge whether a pursuit is worthwhile, models verify the experimental record in the appendix, and human curation decides where the field goes next.

items.title: Imagining Japanese Technofutures – The Role of Futurology and Science Fiction in Shaping the Information Society
items.abstract: The original roots of the information society (jōhō shakai) are clearly Japanese and date back to the year 1963. The concept was developed in the context of a private study group circle spearheaded by the anthropologist Umesao Tadao, including members like the science fiction writer Komatsu Sakyō and the futurologist Hayashi Yūjirō. Drawing on the methodology of science and technology studies (STS), I will show how the ideological narrative underlying Umesao’s original theory on the information industries was condensed into a sociotechnical imaginary (STI) in the years from 1963 to the end of the 1970s. This article explains why the narrative was so successful and how the Expo 1970 in Osaka served as a showcase for the public performance and stabilization of the STI. The article argues that this contributed to its lasting impact on the way in which Japanese technofutures were imagined, based on the premise of a techno-centered society.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Modern Software Development Lifecycle: Methodological Advancements, Developer Productivity, and Quality Engineering
items.abstract: The modern Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) is undergoing a profound paradigm shift driven by the rapid maturation of generative artificial intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), and automated program synthesis engines. While historical transitions—from linear Waterfall models to Agile sprints and continuous DevOps pipelines—focused primarily on procedural orchestration and organizational agility, the integration of Artificial Intelligence introduces cognitive automation directly into the engineering fabric. This research paper presents an exhaustive empirical and methodological investigation into the impact of AI across the end-to-end SDLC, evaluating its tangible ramifications on developer productivity, cognitive workflow dynamics, code quality engineering, and enterprise security. Employing a rigorous triangulated mixed-methods research design, this study combines: (i) quantitative repository mining across 1,200,000 commits spanning 45 enterprise software projects; (ii) a controlled randomized quasi-experiment comprising N = 120 professional software engineers measuring task velocity and cognitive workload via the NASA-TLX inventory; and (iii) longitudinal static analysis tracking post-release defect density and Common Weakness Enumerations (CWE). Our findings demonstrate that AI assistance compresses coding lead times by 55.8% and accelerates developer flow states, yielding substantial improvements across DORA deployment frequency and change velocity metrics. However, ungoverned AI code generation introduces acute quality paradoxes, including a 19.4% surge in code churn, subtle logic regression risks, and elevated vulnerabilities in insecure deserialization and unverified package dependencies. To resolve this tension, we propose a multi-tier Enterprise AI-Augmented SDLC (A-SDLC) Framework coupling Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) policy guardrails, local context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automated mutation test synthesis, and continuous AIOps observability. Finally, we analyze organizational governance imperatives, intellectual property licensing risks, and emerging horizons in autonomous multi-agent coding swarms, establishing an empirical blueprint for resilient, high-assurance software engineering.

items.title: Impact of Virtual Property Tours and Technology on Home-Buying Decisions
items.abstract: Purpose – This paper examines the impact of virtual property tours and allied digital technologies — including 3D/360-degree walkthroughs, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), artificial intelligence (AI)-based recommendation engines and digital mortgage integration — on home-buying decisions. It explores how these technologies are reshaping buyer search behaviour, trust formation, engagement and speed of decision-making, with specific reference to an internship undertaken at House of Real Estate. Design/methodology/approach – The study adopts an exploratory-descriptive design carried out in two phases, a structure informed by the bibliometric-cum-qualitative approach used in prior beauty-influencer marketing research (Shukla and Jha, 2026). Phase I consists of a secondary literature and industry-data review covering global and Indian PropTech adoption trends. Phase II proposes a primary, survey-based investigation to be administered among prospective home buyers and site-visit leads generated by House of Real Estate, structured around the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB). Findings – The secondary evidence indicates that virtual tours and immersive technologies increase listing engagement, shorten time-on-market, encourage remote and out-of-town buyers to shortlist properties faster, and support (but do not replace) the final in-person evaluation before purchase. Adoption is strongest among younger, digitally native buyers and in metro markets, while tier-II/III markets continue to show gaps in digital trust and literacy. Research limitations/implications – The paper is primarily literature- and internship-observation based; the proposed primary survey instrument (Appendix A) requires field administration to generate statistically validated, House of Real Estate-specific results. Findings should therefore be read as a conceptual and directional foundation rather than a conclusive empirical outcome. Originality/value – The paper extends the growing PropTech literature by explicitly linking virtual-tour adoption to the stages of the buyer decision journey, and by translating this into actionable recommendations for a real estate brand's marketing and sales strategy. Keywords – Virtual property tours, PropTech, home-buying decisions, virtual reality, augmented reality, technology adoption, real estate marketing, consumer behaviour.

items.title: Impacto financeiro e fatores associados ao custo das coberturas extraordinárias na equipe de enfermagem hospitalar
items.abstract: RESUMOObjetivo: descrever o perfil e a concentração das coberturas extraordinárias da equipe de enfermagem hospitalar, comparar sua frequência entre grupos de motivos e analisar os fatores associados ao custo por evento. Métodos: estudo longitudinal retrospectivo baseado em registros administrativos individuais de janeiro de 2024 a maio de 2026, em hospital privado de alta complexidade da região Centro-Oeste do Brasil. Dos 2.416 registros identificados, 2.093 compuseram a coorte principal após exclusões sequenciais por categoria não elegível, motivo ou setor não informado, período indefinido e potenciais duplicidades. Os valores foram corrigidos pelo Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo para reais de maio de 2026. O custo por evento foi analisado por modelo linear generalizado com distribuição Gamma e ligação log, e a frequência mensal por grupo gerencial foi comparada por regressão binomial negativa com erros-padrão agrupados por mês. Resultados: o custo real acumulado foi de R$ 468.056,88, com média de R$ 223,63 por evento. Vacâncias e afastamentos prolongados, ausências não programadas e ausências programadas concentraram 91,5% dos eventos e 92,9% dos custos. Vacâncias e afastamentos prolongados tiveram custo unitário ajustado 5,7% menor que as ausências programadas, porém frequência mensal 2,10 vezes maior; as ausências não programadas foram 1,88 vez mais frequentes que as programadas. As coberturas de enfermeiros tiveram custo ajustado 50,0% maior que as de técnicos de enfermagem. Conclusão: o impacto financeiro decorreu sobretudo da recorrência de déficits estruturais e de ausências não programadas, mais do que do custo unitário, que reflete principalmente a tabela de remuneração. A classificação sistemática das causas permite direcionar ações de recrutamento, planejamento de férias, saúde ocupacional e mecanismos internos de cobertura.Palavras-chave: Absenteísmo; Recursos Humanos de Enfermagem no Hospital; Custos Hospitalares; Administração Hospitalar; Admissão e Escalonamento de Pessoal. Financial impact and factors associated with the cost of extraordinary coverage in the hospital nursing workforce ABSTRACTObjective: to describe the profile and concentration of extraordinary coverage in the hospital nursing workforce, compare its frequency across groups of reasons, and analyze factors associated with cost per event. Methods: retrospective longitudinal study based on individual administrative records from January 2024 to May 2026 in a private high-complexity hospital in the Brazilian Midwest. Of 2,416 records identified, 2,093 composed the primary cohort after sequential exclusion of ineligible categories, missing reason or target unit, undefined coverage period and potential duplicates. Monetary values were adjusted by the Brazilian Extended National Consumer Price Index to May 2026 reais. Cost per event was assessed with a generalized linear model with Gamma distribution and log link, and monthly frequency by managerial group was compared with negative binomial regression with standard errors clustered by month. Results: the cumulative real cost was BRL 468,056.88, with a mean of BRL 223.63 per event. Vacancies and prolonged leaves, unplanned absences and planned absences accounted for 91.5% of events and 92.9% of costs. Vacancies and prolonged leaves had a 5.7% lower adjusted unit cost than planned absences, but a 2.10-fold higher monthly frequency; unplanned absences were 1.88 times more frequent than planned absences. Coverage by registered nurses had a 50.0% higher adjusted cost than coverage by nursing technicians. Conclusion: financial impact resulted mainly from the recurrence of structural staffing gaps and unplanned absences rather than from unit cost, which mainly reflects the payment table. Systematic classification of causes can guide recruitment, vacation planning, occupational health and internal coverage mechanisms.Keywords: Absenteeism; Nursing Staff, Hospital; Hospital Costs; Hospital Administration; Personnel Staffing and Scheduling.

items.title: IMPLEMENTATION OF CLOUD-BASED DIGITAL OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY INSPECTION CHECKLIST FOR WORKPLACE SAFETY MONITORING AT PT X
items.abstract: Effective Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) supervision in the industrial sector demands rapid, accurate, and real-time actionable inspection mechanisms. PT X, a steam power generation company, previously relied on a conventional paper-based inspection system, susceptible to reporting delays of 24–48 hours, document loss, and delayed hazard corrective action responses. This community service program aimed to implement a Cloud-Based Digital OHS Inspection Checklist to enhance workplace safety supervision effectiveness and strengthen OHS personnel capacity at PT X. Participatory Action Research (PAR) was employed alongside a One-Group Pretest-Posttest quasi-experimental design. Activities encompassed inspection form redesign, cloud platform development (AppSheet/Google Workspace), intensive training, and field mentoring involving 30 OHS supervisors and auditors. Effectiveness was evaluated through Normalized Gain (N-Gain) and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test analysis, supplemented by inspection time efficiency metrics. Results indicated a significant improvement in participants' knowledge, with mean scores rising from 52.33 to 88.67 (N-Gain = 0.76, high category; p < 0.001). Operational efficiency improved by 74.2%, reducing processing time from 180 to 46 minutes per session. The cloud-based system proved effective in accelerating real-time hazard coordination and reinforcing safety culture at PT X.

items.title: Improving undergraduates study ability of occupational health and occupational medicine comprehensive experiment applying objectives and key results method
items.abstract: Based on the urgent need to cultivate occupational health action ability in recent years, this study adopted the key Objectives and Key Results (OKR) to explore the practical effect of its application in the comprehensive experimental teaching of“Occupational health and occupational medicine (OHOM)”. We made full use of existing teaching resources, promoted the reform of experimental teaching, and improved the experimental teaching level and experimental ability of undergraduate students majoring in preventive medicine. We randomly selected 60 fourth‑year undergraduate students from two classes of the preventive medicine major to carry out the comprehensive experimental teaching of OHOM. The traditional teaching mode and OKR assessment method were used respectively to observe the teaching effect. There were 15 males (50.00%) and 15 females (50.00%) in the control group. There were 17 males (56.67%) and 13 females (43.33%) in the study group. We established an OKR teaching model for the comprehensive dust exposure experiment in the course of OHOM, including the design of teaching procedures, the arrangement of key steps, and specific evaluation methods. Through practical exploration, we found that in the OKR teaching experimental group, 26.67% and 23.33% of students respectively believed that this teaching mode could improve their learning efficiency and comprehensive learning ability. We obtained a certain understanding of students’ mastery of experimental knowledge and found that the experimental group had a significantly greater mastery of experimental knowledge than the control group did, and OKR had an obvious effect on students’ mastery of experimental knowledge. On the other hand, through the OKR teaching method, students’ learning satisfaction is significantly improved. Both traditional teaching mode and OKR evaluation method have good teaching effect, OKR teaching effect is better than traditional teaching method, comprehensive experiment score is significantly higher than traditional method ( P < 0.05). The practical teaching of the OHOM comprehensive experimental course highlights, to a certain extent, the advantages of its professional characteristics, strengthens the teaching of experimental skills, and integrates the OKR assessment method. It can serve as an important supplement to and resource expansion of traditional classroom learning, and holds considerable value for promotion in improving the quality of comprehensive experimental teaching.
